How circumcision became cash cow for churches
items.description: The initiation ground is now a church hall and the admission ticket costs tens of thousands of...
content: Nurses carry out voluntary medical male circumcision procedure on a boy. Every December, thousands of boys disappear into church compounds for one week. They come out circumcised.
At dawn in Eldoret, long before the morning chill lifts over the Rift Valley, a quiet convoy of family cars pulls into a church compound in Maili Nne.

Inside are anxious teenage boys carrying mattresses, basins and Bibles. They are not going to boarding school. This is the modern kit for a rite of passage that once demanded a trek to the riverbank and the steady hand of a village elder.

In Mt Kenya, the scene is almost identical. Every December, thousands of boys disappear into church compounds for one week. They come out circumcised, with a certificate, and evangelised into Christianity.

The initiation ground is now a gated church hall, the surgeon wears medical scrubs, and the admission ticket costs tens of thousands of shillings. Depending on a church’s status, location and the duration of the camp, parents pay between Sh10,000 and Sh50,000 per child.

Kiama Kia Ma national patron Kung’u Muigai laments that “nobody calls it business, they call it ministry”. Economically, he says, it is a seasonal industry worth tens of millions every year, “and it repeats itself like harvest”.
Also Read: Why forced male circumcision audits violate the Constitution
It was not always so. According to Mr Joseph Kaguthi, the convener of elders and the clergy in the joint Council of Elders in Mt Kenya, circumcision belonged to the elders.
“They decided who cuts, when, where, and what the boy is taught. A family paid them with a goat, with beer, with respect. The boy joined an age-set that governed him for life,” he said.
Missionaries broke that order. From the 1920s to the 1950s, he says the Church of Scotland (PCEA), the Catholic Church, among others, banned what they called forest circumcision.

“The missions built hospitals. The doctor replaced the traditional circumciser. The hospital replaced the forest. The elders lost the first battle because they had wisdom but no hospital,” Mr Kaguthi said.
Later, he says, the Mungiki sect and other gangs made home-based healing risky, and boys recuperating at home were recruited into gangs.

“This is the fault line the church took to convince families that it was risky to trust cultural circumcision and proposed the religious cut. The proliferation of single mothers in the community also fuelled the adoption of religious cut,” he said.

Murang’a-based preacher Charity Kagina says, “A church camp is a school compound. It has a fence, a gate, and a watchman. Your son’s name is written down. You get a receipt. The church became the security provider because the state and the elders failed.”
For parents, the bill is real. James Rono of Eldoret paid Sh17,000 to have his son hosted for a one-week camp at a Catholic church.
Also Read: Lukhembe - The sacred blade at the heart of Bukusu circumcision

“We are paying Sh17,000 for a period of less than 14 days. The fee covers the doctor’s charges for the cut, food, accommodation, and the mentorship programme,” he said. “It is expensive in these tough economic times, but as parents, we want our boys to be safe and guided properly.”
Bishop Joseph Kagunda of ACK Mt Kenya West, a pioneer of church-run circumcision, admits the church charges a fee that was up to Sh10,000 in his time and has since risen sharply.
“Besides food, they did not get much in terms of counselling and being guided into the next phase of their lives. Now we teach them about being responsible,” he said.

An Eldoret bishop who asked not to be named said: “Most of us offering the services as churches, we are not after profit. People look at the sum and think the church is making a profit, yet they forget we feed these boys three to four times a day, pay qualified doctors, hire security, and bring in professionals to mentor them.”
Another said: “You cannot put a price tag on saving a boy from drug abuse, radicalisation, and moral decay. We are building responsible men for the church and the nation.”

Even within the church, there is unease. Bishop Wilson Kurui of Jesus Love Ministries in Eldoret supports the initiative but cautions: “This service should not be viewed as an opportunity to generate income but must be used as one of the ways the church is supporting the society.”
The initiation ground is now a gated church hall, the surgeon wears medical scrubs, and the admission ticket costs tens of thousands of shillings.

PCEA’s Rev Hezekiah Murage questions whether the camps produce real manhood or just a certificate, while theologian Dr Samuel Ndogo counters that criticism must be based on evidence, not anecdotes. For the elders, the church’s dominance is cultural erasure dressed in clerical robes.

“Christians must stick to preaching the gospel and leave circumcision to us,” said 91-year-old Thomas Ingara, a Tiriki traditional circumciser from Kalwani village in Hamisi sub-county. “Now, churches are forcing foreign culture into our rites while hiding behind the Bible to collect huge sums of money from poor parents. When you strip a boy of his cultural roots and lock him in a hall for a week, what kind of elder will he become tomorrow?”
Mr Muigai says some parishes invite an elder for a one-hour session.
“But the elder is limited to only greeting the boys. He is given tea and fare home. The elder who once received a whole goat now receives almost nothing,” he said.
Kiama kia Ma proposes that the church teach the boys for one week and the elders for another one week.

“Most churches have refused. Officially, they say elders will teach pagan things. Unofficially, elders say the real reason is money: If elders come in, parents will ask why they are paying Sh20, 000 to the church when elders charge about Sh5,000,” said Mr Muigai.
Bishop Kurui agreed that elders have a place in the process.

Also Read: My nephew died after a botched circumcision, who is liable?
“There are things that pastors cannot articulate well when it comes to circumcision,” he said.
Safety is the other concern. Pastor Isaac Wanakacha, a senior nurse formerly at Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital, advocates for hospital-based circumcision followed by guidance at home.
“Public hospitals and accredited clinics offer very favourable rates, and many facilities even allow parents to use the Social Health Authority (SHA) cover to settle the bills,” he said.
Cultural researcher Mwaura wa Koigi said the church did not win because it had more truth.

“It won because it had secure circumcision venues as well as trusted clergy for mentorship. Mungiki made circumcision dangerous. The church made it safe. Then the church made it profitable,” he argued.

He added that until Mt Kenya creates a model that is safe, affordable and owned by neither a gang nor a church business, the elders will continue to lick the bone outside the circumcision gate, while the church mints millions inside.

items.title: Over One Million Candidates Complete 2026 KCSE Examinations Countrywide
items.description: Over One Million Candidates Complete 2026 KCSE Examinations Countrywide Kenya News Agency CS Ogamba: Expect KCSE, KPSEA results in January; KJSEA in December Daily Nation Curtain falls on 2026 KCSE as candidates sit final Physics practicals The Star, Kenya Education PS praises smooth exam administration, assures schools of Grade 11 preparedness Kenya News Agency Kenya: Principal Secretary,basic Education John Ololtuaa, Monitor Exams in Eldoret Africa.com
content: The 2026 Kenya Certificate of Secondary Education (KCSE) Examinations came to a close, today, with a record 1,048,355 candidates registered across 10,693 examination centres countrywide having sat for their respective papers, thus, marking the first time in the history of a national examination that candidature surpassed the one million marks.

Education Cabinet Secretary (CS), Julius Migos Ogamba, said the milestone reflected the growing number of learners progressing through the country’s education system, with the government deploying a Multi-agency coordination framework, to facilitate the administration of examinations on an unprecedented scale.

Speaking during an inspection and monitoring exercise on the final day of the examinations in Sosiot Town, Belgut Sub-county in Kericho, Ogamba said the exercise had been conducted successfully despite flooding, insecurity and logistical challenges, that threatened to disrupt examination activities in several parts of the country.

The Cabinet Secretary disclosed that the government had effectively facilitated the participation of candidates in affected regions through emergency interventions, maintaining that no candidate had missed an examination paper because of the disruptions.

He identified flooding in Tana River, Kitui, Turkana, West Pokot, Wajir and Mandera counties as one of the major challenges encountered during the examination period, with damaged and inaccessible transport routes, complicating the delivery of examination materials.

Ogamba mentioned few isolated insecurity incidents in Moyale, Isiolo, Dadaab in Garissa County, Kapedo and Arror in Baringo and Turkana Counties, which necessitated additional security arrangements, to safeguard candidates and examination personnel.

To overcome the difficulties, the government deployed helicopters and alternative means of transport to deliver examination materials, to inaccessible areas, while some candidates were temporarily relocated to safer locations, to enable them to sit their papers.

The Cabinet Secretary attributed the successful administration of the exercise to the coordinated efforts of officers from the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Interior and National Administration, the Teachers Service Commission and other government agencies involved in examination management.

He disclosed that examination materials had been distributed daily through 646 designated distribution centres countrywide, with security personnel and education officials working together to facilitate timely delivery to examination centres.
“The dedication of our officers has been very pivotal to the success of this exercise, especially in view of the challenges that we have faced this season,” Ogamba said.

During his visit to Belgut Sub-county, the Cabinet Secretary witnessed the opening of the Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC) examination container at the Deputy County Commissioner’s office in Sosiot Town and the distribution of sealed examination materials to examination centre managers.
He later proceeded to Kabianga Boys Senior School, where he monitored the administration of the final KCSE examination papers to candidates.

Turning to the next Phase of the national examination process, Ogamba announced that an estimated 34,170 examiners, would undertake the marking of KCSE answer scripts across 41 designated marking centres, with the Ministry targeting the release of results in January 2027.

He said the processing of the 2026 Kenya Junior School Education Assessment (KJSEA), had been given priority to facilitate the release of results in December 2026 and the subsequent placement of learners into Grade 10 in senior schools before January 2027.

The Cabinet Secretary disclosed that 13,484 examiners were already marking KJSEA structured questions at 24 marking centres, while multiple-choice questions were being processed concurrently through machine scoring.

He further indicated that the 2026 Kenya Primary School Education Assessment (KPSEA) outcomes would be released in January 2027, to provide feedback on learners’ academic achievement as they transition to Grade 7 in junior school.

The Cabinet Secretary explained that candidates attaining university entry qualifications would have opportunities to pursue degree programmes, while others could advance their education through Technical and Vocational Education and Training institutions, the Kenya Medical Training College and other training institutions.

Ogamba said the Competency-Based Education system was designed to recognize individual abilities by integrating academic achievement with practical skills and talent development, enabling learners to pursue pathways suited to their strengths.

On school financing, the Cabinet Secretary announced that the government was preparing to review capitation rates for primary, junior and senior schools, which have remained unchanged since 2015, to address funding shortfalls affecting learning institutions.

He disclosed that the Ministry of Education would establish a team to examine the existing capitation framework and recommend adjustments, aimed at ensuring schools receive adequate resources to implement their academic programmes.
On budgetary allocations, Ogamba disclosed that government funding for the education sector had increased from approximately Sh500 billion in 2022 to Sh784 billion in the 2026/2027 Financial Year.

He further indicated that the allocation was projected to rise to nearly Sh850 billion in the 2027/2028 Financial Year as the government continues to expand educational infrastructure and strengthen institutional capacity.

Regarding the implementation of Competency-Based Education, Ogamba said the government was undertaking the construction of 1,600 laboratories in senior schools to strengthen practical learning and support the transition of learners to Grade 10.

He explained that the laboratory programme formed part of wider infrastructure investments involving additional classrooms and hostels, to increase the capacity of learning institutions as enrolment continues to rise.

Kericho County Commissioner, Omari Ali, who accompanied the Cabinet Secretary during the inspection, wished the candidates success and encouraged them as they prepare for the next stage of their education.
Also present were Kericho County Director of Education, Julius Ngoneshi and other senior national government, education and security officials.

items.title: From “All Politicians Must Go” to Defending Political Godfathers....How Kenya’s Youth Lost Control of Their Own Movement
items.description: One thing young Kenyans need to confront is how quickly the goalposts have shifted since the 2024 protests. We went from “All Politicians Must Go” to watching the same old...
content: One thing young Kenyans need to confront is how quickly the goalposts have shifted since the 2024 protests. We went from “All Politicians Must Go” to watching the same old politicians dominate political conversations, with young people now fighting over personalities they once rejected.
At what point did the generation that rejected political godfathers become so emotionally attached to those same politicians that questioning them is now considered betrayal?

What happened to the demands for accountability, an end to corruption, reduced government spending and a complete change in how this country is governed? How did we move from rejecting the entire political establishment to defending individual politicians as though they were sent from heaven?

Some young people have become so politically naive that they genuinely believe a candidate surrounded by wealthy political families, powerful establishment figures and people associated with past public finance controversies must automatically have their interests at heart.

We spent years questioning the handling of Eurobond proceeds, the accumulation of unexplained wealth and the political families that have enjoyed enormous influence while ordinary Kenyans struggle to survive. Yet today, some young people barely question the same political networks when they appear behind their preferred candidates.

How does a politician become a symbol of change simply because they have joined the side you support? Does yesterday's political baggage disappear because someone has endorsed your favourite candidate?

The real question is who is setting the agenda today. Is it the young people who started the movement, or the legacy politicians who already control political parties, campaign financing, grassroots networks and the machinery of electoral politics?

Having thousands of people on X Spaces, trending hashtags and making noise online is not the same as controlling a political movement. You can dominate social media for an entire week while someone else makes all the important political decisions.

And any young person who confidently tells you that “We are in control” should explain exactly what decisions young people are making independently of the established political class. Otherwise, they are simply selling you Coke.

What makes this particularly interesting is how quickly the standards change depending on which politician is involved. The corruption that was unacceptable yesterday suddenly becomes a secondary issue when the accused politician joins the preferred political camp.

The 2024 protests were bigger than Ruto, bigger than the opposition and bigger than any political family. They raised fundamental questions about how Kenya is governed, how public money is spent and why ordinary citizens must keep paying for the failures of successive administrations.
Those questions should not disappear because the country is approaching another election.
The most uncomfortable question remains unanswered. Did the political establishment actually change, or did some of the young people who wanted to dismantle it simply find new politicians to defend?

Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi has called on residents of Western Kenya to throw their full support behind President William Ruto ahead of the next general election, arguing that political opposition has historically failed to deliver tangible development to the region.

Speaking in Butere on Friday, November 20, Mudavadi invoked the legacy of the late Martin Shikuku, widely regarded as a standard-bearer of opposition politics in Western Kenya , to make his case that opposition politics cannot be a permanent destination for the region's leaders.

The Prime Cabinet Secretary went further to predict that Ruto would secure a second term in a free and fair election, declaring his full commitment to the partnership with the President.

President Ruto, also speaking at rallies in the region, announced a sweeping package of government investments for Kakamega County under the affordable housing programme. He said the government had committed KSh 21 billion to construct housing units, hostels, and markets across the county.

Specifically, the President said 850 housing units are under construction in Kakamega, alongside a planned 14-storey building and an additional 2,000 units to be built in the area. He added that 20 markets are either complete or ongoing in the county.
Ruto also announced a KSh 3 billion allocation from the Housing Fund to construct hostels for 11,000 university students in Kakamega, with hostels to be built within every constituency.

He dismissed critics who questioned why high-rise construction was being extended to towns such as Butere, arguing that the government had already delivered similar projects in Nairobi, Eldoret, Kisumu, Mombasa, and Machakos.

Kenyans in US await Sifuna’s arrival
items.description: LMM’s diaspora network has organised itself into state chapters across 50 US states.
content: Nairobi Senator and Linda Mwananchi Movement leader Edwin Sifuna during a Sunday service at Jesus Teaching Ministry in Nairobi on October 18, 2026.

As Edwin Sifuna lands in the United States over the Thanksgiving weekend, anticipation is building among Kenyan diaspora communities eager to assess one of the leading contenders in Kenya’s 2027 presidential race.

Beyond the political rallies and fundraising events, many see the visit as an opportunity to engage directly with an aspirant seeking to expand his national appeal and strengthen ties with an increasingly influential constituency abroad. Sifuna’s US trip carries significant political implications, according to Prof Kefa Otiso of Bowling Green State University,
“The diaspora’s most important contribution to these politicians is fundraising for their campaigns and influencing friends and family back home to support them,” says Prof Otiso.
Also Read: How hardliners in Kalonzo, Sifuna camps are complicating opposition talks
Nairobi Senator and Linda Mwananchi movement leader Edwin Sifuna speaking during a Sunday service at Jesus Teaching Ministry in Nairobi, on October 18, 2026.
Sifuna’s tour, like previous visits by Kalonzo Musyoka, David Maraga and Rigathi Gachagua, includes a significant fundraising component.

These visits feature paid events, meet-and-greet sessions, photo opportunities and fundraising drives through WhatsApp mobilisation networks. This has raised the stakes for candidates seeking the presidency in 2027.
On the significance of diaspora funding, Prof Otiso said,

items.title: Gachagua’s green wave: How DCP is reshaping Kenya’s political map ahead of 2027
items.description: Gilgil Member of Parliament Martha Wangari crossed the floor to the Democracy for the Citizens Party on Friday, joining a growing exodus of legislators abandoning the ruling United Democratic Alliance as former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua's opposition movement accelerates its march towards the August 2027 general election with a confidence that is becoming increasingly difficult for the political establishment to dismiss.
content: From Gilgil to Laikipia, a steady stream of legislators, county assemblies and grassroots leaders is rewriting Kenya’s political landscape — and Rigathi Gachagua is betting it all on March.

Gilgil Member of Parliament Martha Wangari crossed the floor to the Democracy for the Citizens Party on Friday, joining a growing exodus of legislators abandoning the ruling United Democratic Alliance as former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua’s opposition movement accelerates its march towards the August 2027 general election with a confidence that is becoming increasingly difficult for the political establishment to dismiss.

Wangari, a member of the National Assembly’s Speaker’s Panel and one of the more recognisable faces in the Mount Kenya parliamentary bloc, formalised her defection at Gachagua’s Wamunyoro residence in a ceremony that drew considerable attention — not least because she was joined by Naivasha MP Jayne Kihara and Kipipiri MP Wanjiku Muhia, two more legislators adding their weight to what DCP is calling a green wave sweeping across central Kenya and beyond.

“The people are supreme,” Gachagua said, framing Wangari’s move not as a personal political calculation but as the execution of a popular mandate. “She has listened to them and acted on their wishes.” He assured her of free and fair nominations ahead of party primaries scheduled for March next year, a promise he has now repeated to every defector who has crossed to DCP — and there have been many.

The numbers are beginning to tell a story. DCP now counts 26 Members of Parliament among its ranks, a tally that would have seemed fanciful when Gachagua was impeached in October 2024 and left office in circumstances that many of his allies described as a politically engineered removal. That the same man is now hosting legislators, county assembly delegations and thousands of grassroots leaders at his private residence, week after week, represents one of the more remarkable political rehabilitations in recent Kenyan history.

Friday’s events at Wamunyoro went beyond the parliamentary defections. The entire Nyandarua County Assembly formally joined DCP, giving Gachagua a complete sweep of that county’s devolved legislative arm. More than 1,000 grassroots leaders attended to present Kiharu parliamentary aspirant Mark Njung’e, who joined other candidates seeking DCP tickets for 2027. The entire Jubilee leadership structure from Kiambu County, led by chairman George Maara, also defected — a symbolically charged move given Jubilee’s historical dominance in the region and its current association with former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i, whom Gachagua identified as a figure with whom DCP maintains a cordial relationship, particularly on the question of identifying a joint presidential candidate.

That detail deserves scrutiny. Gachagua was careful to note that while DCP and Jubilee had agreed on cooperation at the presidential level, they would compete independently in all other positions — a tactical arrangement designed to maximise voter turnout and what he called “vote protection.” It is the language of a politician who has studied the architecture of Kenyan electoral politics carefully and understands that coalition-building at the top means little without grassroots mobilisation at the bottom.

The aspirants arriving at Wamunyoro reflect that understanding. Pastor Victor Mwangi Kanyari, who has settled on a DCP ticket for the Kasarani parliamentary seat, was welcomed alongside John Lemuna, a Laikipia North parliamentary aspirant who arrived accompanied by a ward-level MCA candidate from Segera. These are not headline figures. They are the foot soldiers of any serious electoral machine, and their presence signals that DCP’s recruitment is operating not merely at the level of optics, but at the granular level where elections are actually won and lost.

The political context surrounding all of this is significant. President William Ruto, who shared power with Gachagua for two years before orchestrating his removal, now faces a resurgent former ally who has positioned himself as the authentic voice of the Mount Kenya community and the broader opposition. The relationship between the two men has deteriorated publicly and bitterly. Ruto has accused Gachagua of extortion. Gachagua has accused Ruto of purchasing crowds and running a government without genuine popular support. The mutual antagonism has moved well beyond political rivalry into something that resembles a personal reckoning, and both men appear to understand that August 2027 will be its final arbitration.

Gachagua’s warnings to the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission against vote manipulation — issued during the same week as the Wamunyoro events — are consistent with a campaign strategy that anticipates a contested electoral environment and seeks to place accountability markers early. By raising the spectre of rigging before the campaign has formally begun, he frames any future electoral dispute in terms favourable to his narrative.

Whether the green wave translates into actual votes remains the central question. Kenya’s political history is littered with movements that commanded impressive pre-election momentum and fell short when it mattered. The March party primaries will be the first real test of DCP’s organisational depth, and Gachagua’s repeated promise of free and fair nominations will face its most credible examination then. If the primaries are chaotic, exclusionary or perceived as predetermined, the coalition he is building could fracture before it reaches the general election.

For now, however, the momentum is undeniable. Legislators, county assemblies, grassroots networks and parliamentary aspirants from Gilgil to Laikipia are making the same calculation: that the political future, at least in this particular corner of Kenya, is green. Whether that calculation proves correct will define not only Gachagua’s legacy, but the shape of Kenya’s sixth administration.
The count is growing, the primaries are approaching, and the man at the centre of it all is receiving visitors at Wamunyoro — patient, methodical, and showing no sign of slowing down.

items.title: Canada to Offer 5,500 Slots to Foreign Workers by Making Rural Programme Permanent
items.description: Canada makes the Rural Community Immigration Programme permanent, with 5,500 annual places across 14 communities to tackle persistent rural labour shortages.
content: Elijah Ntongai is an experienced editor at TUKO.co.ke, with more than four years in financial, business, labour and technology reporting. His work provides valuable insights into Kenyan, African, and global trends.
Canada has permanently established a rural immigration pathway designed to help smaller communities address long-standing workforce shortages, the federal government announced on November 9, 2026.

Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab made the announcement in Pictou County, Nova Scotia, confirming that the Rural Community Immigration Pilot has been converted into a permanent programme under the country's 2027–2029 Immigration Levels Plan.
UK Embassy Kenya announces deadline to apply for 2027 fully funded Commonwealth scholarships

The employer- and community-led initiative is structured around local partnerships between businesses and community organisations, with the aim of connecting newcomers and their families to the support networks necessary for long-term settlement.
The government plans to retain the 14 communities currently participating in the pilot, with further expansion to additional communities planned at a later stage.
For the 2027 admissions cycle, the government has set a target of 5,500 spaces under the now-permanent Rural Community Immigration Programme.
The initiative traces its roots to the Rural and Northern Immigration Pilot, which ran from 2019 to 2024 and saw more than 2,800 employers participate.
Over 12,500 candidates and their families were admitted to rural and smaller communities through that pilot.
The current Rural Community Immigration Pilot, launched in 2025, has already shown early impact.
Canada seeks welders and 25 other priority jobs to apply and live in its villages
Between January 2025 and August 2026, participating communities vetted and designated more than 1,950 trusted employers facing persistent labour shortages.
Those employers issued over 4,700 job offers and community recommendations, with newcomers helping to fill vacancies in sectors including health care, education, and sales and services.
Jason Guidry, Chief Executive Officer of Pictou County Partnership, said the permanent status of the programme would give rural regions greater certainty when planning for workforce needs.

Amber Manning, Human Resources Manager at WearWell Garments Limited, a Pictou County manufacturer established in 1978, highlighted the practical value of immigration pathways for businesses struggling to find skilled workers locally.

The programme sits alongside other permanent residence pathways, including the Provincial Nominee Programme and federal economic programmes managed through Express Entry, as well as various temporary immigration routes available to employers across Canada.
In other news, the US Department of State clarified the purposes of its three main passport application forms , warning that submitting the wrong one could delay processing.

Form DS-11 is for first-time applicants, children under 16 and individuals who do not qualify for renewal, while DS-82 is reserved for eligible passport renewals by mail or through the online service.
Form DS-5504 is used to correct or update passport information, change a name or replace a passport originally issued with limited validity.

Applicants can use the State Department's online form guide and fee calculator to identify the correct application, with those applying from outside the US advised to check their nearest American embassy or consulate for country-specific instructions.

content: Kenya has officially flagged off eight competitively selected Kenyan university students participating in the 2026 edition of Huawei’s flagship global Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiative, Seeds for the Future.
The eight Kenyan delegates will travel to Dongguan and Shenzhen, China, for an intensive, fully funded technical immersion.

During their stay, the students will gain hands-on training at Huawei’s state-of-the-art research and development facilities, mastering emerging technologies including Artificial Intelligence (AI), 5G and 6G networks, cloud computing, and digital power systems, while engaging in knowledge exchange with international peers.

Presiding over the ceremonial handover of the Kenya National Flag to the student delegation on Thursday, Principal Secretary, State Department for Foreign Affairs Dr. Korir Sing’Oei, representing the Prime Cabinet Secretary and Cabinet Secretary for Foreign and Diaspora Affairs, Musalia Mudavadi underscored the critical role of human capital development in national growth and global competitiveness.

“Education is the pathway for transformation, but only to the extent that we link education to markets, skills, and job creation. By enabling students of technology and leadership in Kenya to travel to Shenzhen and interact directly with a global technology powerhouse like Huawei, we are providing a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. Huawei’s investment directly strengthens Nairobi’s position as a digital leader on the African continent,” he said.

The PS further noted that this initiative translates key commitments made during his official delegation visit to Huawei Headquarters in Shenzhen in August 2026 into tangible outcomes for Kenyan youth.

He highlighted that the initiative aligns with the Government’s Digital Superhighway agenda under the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA) and reinforces the strategic bilateral friendship between the Republic of Kenya and the People’s Republic of China.
Speaking on behalf of Huawei Technologies Kenya, Sun Quan (James), Deputy Chief Executive Officer, reaffirmed Huawei’s commitment to nurturing local ICT talent.

“This program is named ‘Seeds for the Future.’ As these eight talented students visit Shenzhen to exchange ideas with global technical experts, our hope is that when they return, they will turn into ‘Big Trees’ that contribute significantly to Kenya’s digital economy and national development.”

Launched globally in 2008, Huawei’s Seeds for the Future program has cultivated tech talent across the globe, engaging nearly 19,800 students from 143 countries and building partnerships with over 500 universities worldwide.

The 2026 edition reinforces Huawei’s ongoing support for Kenya’s digital ecosystem, extending across private sector infrastructure, public sector capacity building, and advanced technical skills transfer.

The ceremony was attended by key government and industry leaders, including Amb. Jane B. Makori, Deputy Director General for Asia Affairs; Dr. Wahome Rureri, Deputy Director for Higher Education at the State Department for Higher Education; Khadija Mohamed Ahmed of Huawei Technologies; and student representative Ahmed Rashid from the University of Nairobi Faculty of Law, who delivered remarks on behalf of the selected cohort.

items.title: Nairobi runs on borrowed money: CoB flags Sidian Bank overdraft averaging KSh1.6B a month
items.description: Nairobi County has been maintaining a monthly overdraft facility with Sidian Bank of Kenya averaging KSh1.6B to cover staff salaries, with an outstanding balance of KSh1.54B recorded as at 31 March 2026, the Controller of Budget has flagged in a report raising fresh concerns about the county's chronic dependence on short-term borrowing to meet its most basic financial obligations.
content: Nairobi County is financing its monthly wage bill through a rolling bank overdraft — and the Controller of Budget says the arrangement has cost taxpayers millions in charges and penalties.

Nairobi County has been maintaining a monthly overdraft facility with Sidian Bank of Kenya averaging KSh1.6B to cover staff salaries, with an outstanding balance of KSh1.54B recorded as at 31 March 2026, the Controller of Budget has flagged in a report raising fresh concerns about the county’s chronic dependence on short-term borrowing to meet its most basic financial obligations.

Controller of Budget Margaret Nyakang’o’s report reveals that the County Executive has relied on the Sidian Bank overdraft facility specifically to cover personnel emoluments, with the outstanding balance standing at KSh1.54B by 31 March 2026. The county also carried an additional overdraft of KSh214.51M with Co-operative Bank.

Nyakang’o confirmed the arrangement before the Senate Standing Committee on Information Communication and Technology on Monday, noting that the commercial bank had confirmed the facility enabled the county to settle salary payments up to October 2026. She further recommended integrating gratuity into the payroll system and ensuring timely submission of monthly salary requisitions — basic financial hygiene that the county has consistently struggled to maintain.

Beyond the overdrafts, Nairobi still carries a long-standing KSh4.5B loan from Kenya Commercial Bank secured in 2010 under the defunct Nairobi City Council, which remains classified under trade payables — a debt so old it predates devolution, yet one that continues to weigh on a county that spent KSh32.12B on development and recurrent programmes in the reporting period, representing 136 per cent of funds actually released by the Controller of Budget.

That a city generating billions in revenue each year cannot pay its workers without a rolling commercial overdraft is not a fiscal footnote. It is an indictment — and with Nairobi’s 2027 election politics already heating up, the question of who bears responsibility for the financial mess at City Hall is about to become very uncomfortable for everyone inside it.

ODM party leader Oburu Oginga offered Kenyans a rare look inside his private residence after welcoming youth leader and political mobiliser Oketch Salah for a lunch visit on Friday, November 20.
Salah marked the occasion by sharing two photos on social media, capturing the two men in relaxed, candid conversation at different spots within Oburu's home.

The first photo places the pair on a spacious open-air balcony, standing side by side, holding hands and smiling at the camera. Salah turned up in a long white kanzu paired with white sneakers, while Oburu kept to his signature style in a brown and orange diamond-patterned long-sleeved shirt, black trousers, grey slip-on shoes and a grey flat cap.

The balcony itself is quite the setting. Large glossy white tiles cover the floor, with faint grey marble veining running through them. A black wrought-iron railing with ornate scrollwork, curved swirls and interlocking circles frames the edge.

Behind the two men stretches a wall of dense greenery, with tall palm fronds and leafy trees rising under a bright blue sky dotted with a few white clouds. It is the kind of spot designed for unhurried conversation.

Inside, the second photo shows the two men seated in what looks like a classic family living room, far removed from the stiffness of a political office. Salah sits in a cream-coloured plush armchair to the left, animated as he makes a point, while Oburu is relaxed on a larger beige sofa with dark wooden armrests, listening attentively.
Between them sit two round coffee tables with white marble tops and striking gold metal bases, one holding a glass of water.

The room is finished with light blue and sheer white curtains letting in natural light, a large abstract wall painting in gold and brown tones, decorative gold vases on a side table, and a patterned throw draped over the sofa.
Accompanying the photos was a heartfelt message from Salah.
Oburu took over as ODM party leader following the death of his younger brother, Raila Odinga , on October 15.
Since stepping into the role, he has been receiving delegations, youth leaders and party allies at his home as he works to consolidate ODM and define its path forward.
Salah, known for his "Tunataka Pawa!" rallying call for youth empowerment, has been among his most prominent supporters.

We also highlighted facts about President William Ruto’s meeting with the ODM leader , where they discussed strengthening the ODM-UDA partnership and promoting national cohesion.

The talks came weeks after Oburu’s hospital discharge and days after his return to the Senate, where colleagues gave him a standing ovation. He had earlier dismissed rumours of his death, saying they made him “stronger and more determined” to fight his illness.

items.title: UK Embassy in Nairobi celebrates King’s birthday by honouring Kenyan sports personalities
items.description: The United Kingdom Embassy in Nairobi celebrated King Charles III birthday party , who turned 78, by honouring Kenyan sportsmen and women on Thursday evening.
content: The United Kingdom Embassy in Nairobi celebrated King Charles III birthday party , who turned 78, by honouring Kenyan sportsmen and women on Thursday evening.
The UK celebrated close diplomatic ties and collaboration in enhancing sports in Kenya and the critical role of Kenya in Commonwealth sports.
British High Commissioner to Kenya Matt Baugh delivered the keynote address and the King’s message, reaffirming their continued support for the growth of Kenya’s sports globally.
Matt also congratulated Kenya on winning the hosting rights for the 22nd World Athletics Championships in 2029, the first African country to stage the global event.

“And as we’ve heard, the largest ever Kenyan team for a Commonwealth Games, 12 medals in all, three Kenyan flags, proclaiming complete dominance of the men’s Steeplechase. In September, another athletics triumph over the Brits, as Nairobi is awarded the 2029 World Athletics Championships, the first on African soil—the first African country to stage the global event,” the ambassador noted.

Foreign Affairs PS Korir Sing’oei, who delivered the Kenyan government’s message, hailed the strong diplomatic ties between Kenya and the UK in various sectors, among them sports, trade, and education. He reassured that Kenya will continue working with the UK to open more opportunities for the benefit of the two nations.

“The Kenya-UK partnership has been carried forward by successive generations, each passing the baton with care to the next. Kenya reaffirms its commitment to running the next leg with ambition, guided by the values of fair play, mutual respect, shared prosperity, and the enduring friendship between our peoples.” stated the PS

Sing’oei also congratulated Team Kenya’s recent performance at the 23rd Commonwealth Games in Scotland, UK, especially the dominant performance in the men’s 3,000m steeplechase where Edmund Serem led the country to a clean podium sweep.

“The Kenya-UK Economic Partnership Agreement has, since 2021, secured duty-free, quota-free access for Kenyan exports to the British market, and in July 2025, the renewal of the strategic partnership by our two leaders in London.”said the PS

The UK also honoured Kenyan sportsmen and women who have excelled on the global stage, such as recently crowned New York City Marathon champion Sheila Chepkirui, former 800m World and Commonwealth champion Mary Moraa, Kenya Lionesses captain Sheila Chajira, and para-athlete Henry Wanyoike, among others.
King Charles III’s 78th birthday was celebrated in the UK on the 14th of this month.

items.title: Manchester United Training Drone Footage: What Pochettino’s First Session Showed
items.description: See what Manchester United Training Drone Footage captured during Mauricio Pochettino’s first Manchester United training session, the players involved and the Liverpool team news.
content: Manchester United training drone footage captured part of Mauricio Pochettino’s first session with the squad at Carrington on Thursday, 19 November 2026. Around 12 minutes of video appeared online, showing small-group drills and the new head coach working with players. The footage prompted questions about training-ground privacy and how much Liverpool could learn before their Premier League meeting. Here is what the recording, the club’s official team news and the reported accounts establish.

Mauricio Pochettino’s first Manchester United training session took place as the club prepared to visit Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday, 22 November, with kick-off scheduled for 19:30 East Africa Time. The Argentine had arrived in Manchester on Wednesday after completing his final assignment with the United States national team. His first on-pitch work was filmed by an independent drone operator and later published on YouTube. United also released its own training update, confirming the involvement of two players whose availability had been in doubt.

The video of Pochettino’s first Man Utd training session shows football exercises rather than a confirmed tactical plan for Liverpool. Sky Sports reported that the 12-minute recording begins with rondos, in which players circulate possession while others attempt to intercept, before showing Pochettino guiding a smaller group through work on an adjoining pitch. The footage was recorded from outside the training complex and published online by a drone operator identified as CC Overview.

BBC Sport identified multiple groups of players involved in the session, including younger footballers and regular first-team names. Their presence confirms participation in that part of training, not a place in Sunday’s starting eleven.

Manchester United team news ahead of Liverpool received a more reliable update from the club itself: Harry Maguire and Patrick Dorgu trained at Carrington on Thursday. Maguire had been substituted with a back spasm during the 4-4 draw against Aston Villa, while Dorgu had not featured in Denmark’s recent international matches. Their participation is encouraging, but match readiness and selection remain decisions for the coaching staff.

The club also stated that Lisandro Martinez was available after suspension. It planned Pochettino’s first pre-match press conference for Friday, when a fuller assessment of the squad could be provided.

Questions about Mauricio Pochettino’s Manchester United tactics intensified because the footage shows a small group being coached separately from other players. Sky Sports described positional work and a group briefing, but cautioned that those involved should not be assumed to be the starting line-up. Early-session exercises can illustrate a coach’s methods without establishing his match plan.

Pochettino has previously favoured high-intensity work, pressing and collective movement, yet one filmed session cannot show whether those principles will be adopted immediately or how United will line up at Anfield. Any detailed formation claim would need stronger evidence, such as a confirmed team sheet or the manager’s own explanation.

The Carrington filming controversy centres on the publication of training images that the club had not itself released. Reports said the operator maintained that the drone was flown in unrestricted airspace, stayed within visual range and complied with the relevant requirements. Sky Sports also reported that signs near the complex prohibit drones and that Manchester United declined to comment on the incident.

Those accounts establish a dispute about access and privacy, not a legal determination. Nor is there evidence that Liverpool commissioned the recording or that the video changed either team’s preparations.

Liverpool vs Manchester United on 22 November 2026 is scheduled to be Pochettino’s first match as United head coach, only days after his appointment. United enter the trip amid pressure to improve their Premier League performances, while the manager has called for a brave approach to the Anfield encounter. The Manchester United fixtures and results hub covers the club’s wider schedule.

The recording adds another story to a busy opening week for the Argentine, but his early results and team selections will offer better evidence of his approach than isolated training footage. Read our Pochettino Manchester United overview for the appointment and immediate Premier League challenge. For current match scores, fixtures and standings, follow SportPesa Score.

Pochettino’s first Manchester United session became news because 12 minutes of training were recorded from the air and shared publicly. The footage shows on-pitch work and player groupings; it does not confirm Sunday’s line-up or prove that the club’s tactical plans were exposed. With Maguire and Dorgu back in training, attention now turns to the final team news and the Liverpool fixture. The outcome at Anfield will provide the first competitive measure of this new chapter at United.

items.description: Morgan Bahati debuts with ‘Zoza’ as veteran musician Bahati steps back from music to pursue a Mathare MP bid, after waiting for him to choose his own path.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.
Kenyan music veteran Bahati has proudly introduced his eldest son, Morgan Bahati, to the music world, with the teenager dropping his debut single, Zoza, on November 20, 2026.
The song, which carries the subtitle Nikifika 18, premiered at noon on the Bahati Kenya YouTube channel, marking a significant milestone for the family.
The timing was no coincidence: Bahati has also confirmed he is stepping away from active music to concentrate on his bid to become the Member of Parliament for Mathare.

In an Instagram post announcing the launch, Bahati revealed that Morgan had harboured a passion for music from a very young age, almost certainly inspired by watching his father build one of Kenya's most recognisable music careers.

Despite that, Bahati chose not to rush the process.
The wait appears to have been worth it. Bahati was clearly delighted with what he saw, noting that Morgan came across as composed, fluent and confident, even managing to outdo his father's English.
The debut also signals a shift in direction for Bahati himself.

The gospel-turned-pop star, who has been a prominent name in Kenyan entertainment for over a decade, is now setting his sights on the Mathare constituency, taking a sabbatical from his music career to pursue his political ambitions.
Handing Morgan the spotlight at this particular moment feels deliberate: a passing of the torch as the elder Bahati pivots to a new chapter.
Morgan, still in high school, now steps into the public eye on his own terms, with a debut that his father has been carefully nurturing behind the scenes.
Whether Morgan can carve out his own identity beyond his famous surname remains to be seen, but the foundation has clearly been laid with great care.

Elsewhere, Bahati denied duping Kenyans with a wedding during an appearance on NTV's Fixing The Nation, explaining that his hyped "Bahati's Big Day" campaign was a deliberate month-long marketing strategy to build demand and launch his 2027 Mathare MP bid.
He disclosed that the event raised KSh 10 million , with contributions varying widely, which was directed toward his Bahati Cares initiative supporting families nationwide.

Bahati maintained that the public only assumed it was a wedding because he left the nature of the day open, insisting the attention generated proved his reach as an entertainer and connection to Mathare.

Kenya’s cabinet secretary honoured with Global Alliance- APRA’s Global Icon Award
items.description: Hon. Kabogo has championed the understanding that government communication must go beyond announcements and information dissemination.
content: Hon. Kabogo’s leadership reflects a commitment to modernising government communication through digital platforms, strengthening stakeholder engagement, embracing innovation, and fostering a more responsive and citizen-centred approach to public information.

Kenya’s Cabinet Secretary, Hon. William Kabogo, has been honoured with the prestigious Global Icon in Artificial Intelligence, Public Relations & Digital Economy Leadership Award by the Global Alliance and the Africa Public Relations Association in Abuja, Nigeria.

The award recognises his visionary leadership, transformative policy execution, and pioneering contributions to Artificial Intelligence, national connectivity, digital transformation, and the advancement of Kenya’s digital economy.

The recognition celebrates Hon. Kabogo’s commitment to positioning Kenya at the forefront of the Fourth Industrial Revolution through the promotion of responsible and ethical AI, expanded digital infrastructure, innovation, and an enabling environment for technology-driven enterprise, digital skills, and economic opportunity.
Beyond technology and infrastructure, the award places particular emphasis on his contribution to the evolving role of public relations and public communication in modern governance.

Hon. Kabogo has championed the understanding that government communication must go beyond announcements and information dissemination. It must be a deliberate process of engaging citizens, listening to their concerns, building understanding, strengthening institutional credibility, and ensuring that public policies and programmes are communicated in ways that are accessible, relevant, and meaningful to the people they serve.

His approach underscores the growing importance of strategic public relations in government—not merely as a publicity function, but as an essential pillar of governance, public participation, accountability, trust-building, and national development.

In an era defined by rapid technological change, information disorder, and increasingly discerning citizens, effective public communication has become critical to the success of public policy. Hon. Kabogo’s leadership reflects a commitment to modernising government communication through digital platforms, strengthening stakeholder engagement, embracing innovation, and fostering a more responsive and citizen-centred approach to public information.

The recognition also celebrates his efforts to strengthen Kenya’s digital ecosystem through expanded broadband connectivity, support for innovation and technology startups, digital inclusion, and international cooperation. These initiatives are helping create opportunities for citizens and businesses while supporting Kenya’s ambitions as a competitive digital economy.

The award further acknowledges his role in advancing a progressive national narrative—one that communicates Kenya’s ambitions, achievements, opportunities, and place in the global technology landscape with confidence and purpose.

By bringing together Artificial Intelligence, digital economy leadership, and Public Relations, the award recognises a broader vision of modern governance: one in which technological progress is matched by effective communication, innovation by inclusion, and policy ambition by public understanding and trust.

Hon. Kabogo’s recognition in Abuja is not only a personal honour but also a moment of pride for Kenya, affirming the country’s growing influence in digital transformation, strategic communication, innovation, and technology-driven development.
Distinguished African Leaders Among Award Recipients

The award ceremony also recognised an outstanding group of distinguished African leaders and public figures whose contributions to governance, leadership, public service, communication, and national development have earned them various honours.
Among the other recipients recognised at the ceremony were:
-Her Excellency Dr. Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah, President of the Republic of Namibia.
-Rt. Hon. Alban Sumana Bagbin, Speaker of Parliament, Republic of Ghana.
-Alhaji Idris Mohammed, FNIPR, FAPRA, Honourable Minister of Information and National Orientation, Federal Republic of Nigeria.
-Hon. William Kabogo Gitau, EGH, Cabinet Secretary for Information, Communications and the Digital Economy, Republic of Kenya.
-Hon. Dr. Omphile Marupi, Deputy Minister of Information, Publicity and Broadcasting Services Republic of Zimbabwe.
-Hon. Cornelius Mweetwa, former Minister of Information and Media, Republic of Zambia.
-Hon. Felix Kwakye Ofosu, Minister for Government Communications, Republic of Ghana.
-Dr. Shadrick Namalomba, Government Spokesperson and Minister of Information and Communications Technology, Republic of Malawi.

The presence and recognition of such eminent personalities underscored the continental significance of the occasion and celebrated the diverse contributions of African leaders and practitioners to governance, public communication, institutional leadership, and development.

The gathering also highlighted the growing importance of strategic communication, public relations, digital innovation, and leadership in shaping Africa’s future and strengthening the continent’s voice on the global stage.

items.title: Testing a trading app on your phone? Six tech checks Kenyan users should make first
items.description: Trading apps can open up markets that were once out of reach for ordinary Kenyans, from Nairobi Securities Exchange shares to global stocks
content: Kenya’s fintech scene moves fast. M-Pesa changed how the country pays for things, digital lenders changed how it borrows, and now trading apps are changing how a growing number of Kenyans invest. Downloads have climbed as young users look for ways to grow their money beyond SACCOs and savings accounts.

Most coverage of these apps focuses on returns and strategies. This piece looks at something more basic: the technology itself. A trading app holds your identity documents, your money and often access to your M-Pesa line. That makes its security and performance just as important as its features.

Only install trading apps from the Google Play Store or the Apple App Store. Fraudsters regularly circulate APK files through WhatsApp and Telegram that look exactly like legitimate apps but are built to steal login details and one-time passwords. On the store page, check the developer name, the number of downloads, the date of the last update and whether reviews mention withdrawal problems.

Then check the company behind it. In Kenya, the Capital Markets Authority licenses stockbrokers and online forex brokers and publishes the list on its website. Matching the app’s developer to a licensed firm takes two minutes and filters out most scams.

A trading app needs your camera for KYC, internet access and notifications. It has no good reason to read your SMS inbox, your contacts or your call logs. Some fake investment apps request these permissions to intercept M-Pesa messages or harass contacts. On Android, review permissions under Settings, then Apps, and switch off anything that does not make sense.

At minimum, the app should support two-factor authentication through an authenticator app or SMS, and biometric login with fingerprint or face unlock. Authenticator apps are safer than SMS codes, which can be exposed through SIM swap fraud, a problem Kenyan banks and telcos have warned about for years. If an app only offers a simple password, keep looking.

Many trading apps are designed in Europe or Asia and tested on fast connections. In Kenya, users switch between Safaricom, Airtel and home Wi-Fi, and data bundles matter. Test the app on mobile data before funding it. Watch how quickly prices update, whether charts lag, and how the app behaves when the connection drops in the middle of an order. A good app tells you clearly whether an order went through. A poor one leaves you guessing.
Data use is worth checking too. Live charts and streaming prices can consume a surprising amount of a daily bundle, so look for settings that reduce chart refresh rates or switch to a lighter mode.

M-Pesa deposits are now standard among apps that target Kenya, but integration quality varies. The best apps use official Safaricom payment channels with a recognisable paybill or till number and send clear confirmation messages. Be wary of apps that ask you to send money to a personal number or an agent. Test withdrawals with a small amount before depositing more. How quickly and smoothly money comes back tells you a lot about the platform.

Once the basics are covered, compare features. Useful ones include demo accounts with virtual funds, price alerts, clear charting tools, stop-loss orders, transparent fee breakdowns and in-app support that responds within hours, not days. A wider comparison of trading apps in Kenya , with features set out side by side, can help narrow the list. Use it alongside the CMA register rather than in place of it.

Trading apps can open up markets that were once out of reach for ordinary Kenyans, from Nairobi Securities Exchange shares to global stocks. But the same convenience that makes them attractive makes them a target for fraud. Treat a new trading app the way you would treat a new banking app: verify who built it, lock it down, and test it with small amounts before trusting it with your savings.

items.title: Kenya exploring AI application to improve healthcare delivery
items.description: Kenya exploring AI application to improve healthcare delivery Kenya News Agency
content: The Ministry of Health is stepping-up efforts to integrate Artificial Intelligence into healthcare delivery, while strengthening doctors’ welfare and expanding access to HIV prevention services through strategic partnerships.

Principal Secretary (PS) for Medical Services, Dr Ouma Oluga, held a series of engagements at Afya House in Nairobi with representatives of global health organisations, technology experts and the Kenya Medical Practitioners, Pharmacists and Dentists Union (KMPDU), to explore ways of improving healthcare delivery and strengthening the country’s health system.

In a meeting with Ms. Anne Stake, Global Health Team Lead, at Anthropic BPC, the Ministry explored opportunities to harness artificial intelligence (AI) to improve clinical decision-making, disease surveillance, diagnostic efficiency and overall healthcare delivery.

The discussions come as Kenya accelerates its digital health transformation through the Digital Health Agency (DHA), which is spearheading efforts to strengthen digital infrastructure and equip healthcare workers with technology-driven tools to support more informed clinical decisions.

Oluga emphasised the importance of ensuring that AI applications in healthcare align with Kenya’s national AI in Health Strategy, particularly on data sovereignty, security and responsible technology use.

The engagement also highlighted the potential of AI to strengthen health systems while ensuring that emerging technologies are deployed in ways that protect patient information and support sustainable healthcare delivery.
Stake is in Kenya to engage healthcare workers and county health teams in Machakos and Nairobi as part of efforts to understand opportunities and challenges in applying AI to healthcare.
In a separate meeting, Oluga hosted KMPDU officials led by Secretary General, Dr Davji Atellah, to discuss doctors’ welfare and strengthen cooperation between the Ministry and the union.
The PS reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to constructive dialogue and sustained engagement with medical practitioners, recognising their critical contribution to healthcare service delivery.

The discussions focused on promoting the welfare of doctors and addressing issues affecting healthcare professionals, with both sides underscoring the importance of collaboration in improving the quality of health services.

Oluga also held talks with a delegation from the Elton John AIDS Foundation (EJAF) and Tiko Africa on strengthening sustainable HIV prevention programmes through increased national ownership, predictable financing and strategic partnerships.

He called for expanded access to HIV prevention services, particularly among populations at substantial risk, while urging development partners to align their support with national health priorities and strengthen existing health systems.

The meeting also examined emerging HIV prevention technologies, including long-acting injectable Lenacapavir, with Oluga stressing the need for scientific evidence, affordability, regulatory compliance and adequate health-system preparedness before their wider adoption.
The engagement explored opportunities to strengthen HIV prevention programmes, generate evidence and introduce innovative approaches to service delivery.
The delegation was led by EJAF Chief Executive Officer Anne Aslett and Tiko Africa Co-Chief Executive Officer Serah Malaba, alongside representatives from the two organisations.

The engagements reflect the Ministry’s broader focus on combining digital innovation, improved healthcare workforce welfare and strategic partnerships to build a resilient, accessible and sustainable health system.

items.title: TikTok, ICC Kenya to equip creators with digital commerce skills
items.description: Kenyan digital creators are set to gain digital commerce skills to help them scale up and reach wider number of online consumers.
content: Kenyan digital creators are set to gain digital commerce skills to help them scale up and reach wider number of online consumers.
This follows the launch of the first flagship Digital Commerce Labs (DCL) by TikTok and the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC).
Under the partnership, TikTok and ICC target to train thousands of small businesses across Sub-Saharan Africa in digital commerce skills which will be delivered both online and offline

“Digital commerce is reshaping how businesses grow across Sub-Saharan Africa, and Kenyan entrepreneurs are at the heart of that shift,” said Kushal Prakash, TikTok Head of Global Institution Engagement.
Prakash said social commerce has the power to unlock opportunities, level the playing field and equip Kenyan entrepreneurs with the tools to grow.

“Through our partnership with ICC, we are committed to making sure that the benefits of that transformation reach every small business owner in this region. We have seen how TikTok makes it easier for businesses to be discovered and influence purchase decisions through trends such as #TikTokMadeMeBuyIt,” he added.
Kenya was picked as the first country to kick off the programme given the fact that the country’s cocial commerce is among the fastest growing in the world.
According to GSMA, 49% of Kenyan businesses sell online exclusively through social media, with a further 13% combining social platforms with a website or marketplace.

Head of Presidential Special Projects and Creative Economy Dennis Itumbi challenged the social media giant to avail features such as TikTok Shops to help grow small businesses as part of the programme.

“TikTok Shops is not available in any country in Africa. Kenya is willing to become the pilot market for TikTok Shops. Give us a timeline and tell us what we need to do so that we have TikTok Shops because why then are you training our people if they cannot benefit from those commerce and trade aspects that you already have on your platform,” said Itumbi.
DCL Offer a comprehensive, two-part learning experience designed to help Kenyan businesses harness the full potential of digital commerce.

Participants can access self-taught online modules, developed by local experts and covering topics from building a digital presence and creating effective content, to leveraging AI-driven e-commerce tools and preparing for both domestic and international growth.
The programme will further help Kenyan entrepreneurs and businesses explore real-world digital commerce growth opportunities.

items.title: Edna Karijo Wins Women In Tech Leadership Award At Africa Tech Festival 2026
items.description: Kenya’s Edna Karijo has won the Women in Tech Leadership Award at the Africa Tech Festival Awards 2026
content: Edna Karijo, Associate Director at eMobilis Technology Training Institute, has won the Women in Tech Leadership Award at the Africa Tech Festival Awards 2026. The winners were announced at a gala evening in Cape Town on 18 November, during the 2026 edition of Africa Tech Festival.

The award recognises women who have shown innovation, excellence and leadership in technology across the continent. Edna was shortlisted alongside Majda Lahlou Kassi of Ericsson and Shireen Powell of Project Isizwe.

Karijo leads digital skilling and inclusion work at eMobilis where she has led transformative programmes including Google’s Digital Skills for Africa, Ajira Digital Program and the Norwegian Refugee Council’s area-based livelihoods digital skills initiative. She is also a co-author of She Leads , a book of lessons from women leaders. She was also among the 2025 CIO Africa’s Top 45 Most Influential Women In Digital Transformation.

“This recognition represents far more than a personal achievement,” said Edna Karijo. “It has been a journey of dedicating many years to advocating for access to digital skills, digital inclusion, empowering communities, and creating opportunities for youth, young women, and underserved populations to benefit from technology. All this was made possible through the work at eMobilis Mobile Technology Institute and Internet Society Kenya.”

Edna also congratulated the other winners and thanked the Africa Tech Festival organisers and judges, as well as her family, colleagues, partners and networks. “This recognition belongs to all of us,” she said.

David Monaghan, Vice-President of Africa Tech Festival, said the quality of this year’s entries reflects the depth of Africa’s technology ecosystem, from multinationals to start-ups building impactful platforms.

items.title: Uganda tightens Ebola controls in 34 DRC border districts
items.description: The rules cover gatherings, returning travellers, aid workers and public facilities, while Kenya’s outbreak remains linked to one reported cluster.
content: The rules cover gatherings, returning travellers, aid workers and public facilities, while Kenya’s outbreak remains linked to one reported cluster.

Uganda has tightened controls in 34 high-risk districts bordering the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), requiring health ministry clearance for mass gatherings and 21 days of quarantine or monitored self-isolation for Ugandans returning from the DRC. The measures took effect immediately and are intended to reduce the risk of Ebola crossing the border.

The restrictions were set out in a public health advisory on November 19 by Ministry of Health Permanent Secretary Diana Atwine. Both Capital FM and The Star reported that Uganda’s National Task Force on Epidemic Preparedness and Response approved the measures after assessing the risk from the outbreak in the DRC. Atwine said authorities had seen continued movement across the border, including through unofficial crossing points. She also said earlier restrictions remain in force.

In the designated districts, local authorities are to monitor new arrivals and people moving into communities. Local Council chairpersons must be notified of those movements. People who cross illegally, and those who help them, may face legal action.

The gathering rule is more specific than a blanket ban. Concerts, festivals, political rallies and similar events cannot proceed in the districts without written clearance from the Ministry of Health. The Star’s headline describes the events as suspended, while its report, like Capital FM’s, says they require prior approval. Neither account says all gatherings have been prohibited outright.

Returning Ugandans must undergo health risk assessments before quarantine or monitored self-isolation. Humanitarian workers need clearance from the Director General of Health Services to cross the border, and moving bodies into or out of Uganda also requires government authorisation. Day scholars travelling between the two countries in the designated districts are barred from crossing; boarding students with possible exposure must complete 21 days in designated quarantine facilities before returning to school.

Airports, accommodation and public facilities are also covered. Entebbe International Airport has enhanced screening for arriving and departing passengers, and travellers must complete locator forms before boarding. Airlines and other transport operators risk sanctions if they knowingly carry people without proper authorisation or documentation. Hotels must keep guest registers and verify identification. Schools, health facilities, transport terminals, places of worship and other public facilities must provide handwashing facilities and follow infection-prevention measures. Radio stations in the affected districts must devote at least two hours a month to Ebola-prevention campaigns.

The accounts largely agree on the scope and terms of the restrictions. Capital FM gives extra detail on the instructions to local leaders and the monitoring of hotels and schools. The Star supplies the clearest account of the Kenyan outbreak: it reports that the first case was confirmed on October 6, after a traveller came through Uganda from the DRC; the patient died in Nairobi on October 5. The Star says Kenya recorded nine cases and two deaths , all linked to one transmission cluster, with no evidence of community transmission.

Capital FM says Kenya was approaching the end of its Ebola monitoring period, but the report provided cuts off before giving an end date or further details. The Star does not give a monitoring-period deadline. That leaves the status and timing of the end of monitoring unclear in these accounts.

Only two outlets in this coverage have reported the new measures, so the available reporting is narrow. Both describe an extensive set of controls, but neither says how long they will remain in force or how compliance will be enforced beyond the stated penalties and sanctions. Those details, and whether the rules will prevent further cross-border transmission, are still open.

items.title: Alcohol Use Among Young People Raises Public Health Concerns in Kenya
items.description: By Melisa Mong’ina   Nairobi, Kenya: Alcohol intake among young adults is raising public health concerns in the country, with university students
content: Nairobi, Kenya: Alcohol intake among young adults is raising public health concerns in the country, with university students recording higher levels of consumption and addiction than the general population.

A 2024 study by the National Authority for the Campaign Against Alcohol and Drug Abuse (NACADA) found that alcohol use was higher among university students, at 18.6%, compared with 3.8% among secondary school students and 2.6% among primary school pupils. The study also found that 8.7% of university students had severe alcohol use disorder.

Speaking during a virtual discussion on alcohol control legislation organised by NCD Alliance Kenya, NACADA, Students Campaign Against Drugs (SCAD) and the International Institute for Legislative Affairs (IILA), Adrian Njenga of NACADA warned that early exposure to alcohol could increase the risk of addiction and the use of other substances.
“Alcohol and tobacco are referred to as the gatekeepers or the initiators into the drug world for young people,” said Njenga.

Dr. Catherine Karekezi from NCD Alliance Kenya highlighted that alcohol is a major risk factor for non-communicable diseases, including heart conditions and certain cancers, as well as mental health problems.

“Alcohol is toxic. It is a psychoactive agent. It is a dependence-producing substance that has been classified as a Group One carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer,” Dr. Karekezi said.
She also warned about the effects of alcohol on young people, saying their developing brains make them particularly vulnerable to its long-term effects.
“If we have adolescents and young adults exposed to alcohol consumption, this increases the likelihood of dependency on alcohol,” she added.
Dr. Karekezi underscored that alcohol dependence can also push Kenyan households into poverty, affecting families and the country’s economic development.

Benjamin Odhiambo, a public health expert at the Students Campaign Against Drugs (SCAD) also supported raising the minimum drinking age to 21, arguing that delaying exposure to alcohol could reduce the risk of addiction.
“The earlier an individual is introduced or initiated into substance use, the more likely they are to graduate into problematic alcohol use and then alcohol use disorder,” he said.
Odhiambo added that raising the legal age for drinking and handling alcohol would help protect young people.

He also raised concerns about young people’s exposure to alcohol advertising on social media platforms, stressing that stronger controls on advertising and better tracking of alcoholic products could help protect them and other consumers.
“This shows that we do not have sufficient protections for young people in terms of exposure to these particular products, especially alcohol,” said Odhiambo.

According to Caleb Mbugua of the International Institute for Legislative Affairs (IILA), the proposed Alcoholic Drinks and Drugs Control Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, seeks to raise the minimum legal drinking age from 18 to 21 to protect the health of young people.
He explained that the proposed changes would also prevent people below the new legal age from obtaining alcohol licences or working in places where alcoholic drinks are sold or handled.

The bill would also restrict their access to areas where alcohol is manufactured, stored or consumed, and prohibit the sale of alcoholic drinks to them or to anyone accompanied by people below the new legal age.
“There will be warning signs and notices reflecting the new age limit and alcohol outlets will not be allowed to admit underage customers, whether they are alone or accompanied,” said Mbugua.
